Functional Analysis

This is an introduction to functional analysis. The subject is abstract — definition follows definition, and it is easy to finish a chapter without knowing what we are actually trying to do. So each chapter opens with the intuition and motivation before the precise definitions, theorems and proofs; Chapter 0 draws the overall map, and the last chapter ties the main thread back together.

Background assumed: linear algebra and real analysis (\varepsilon-\delta arguments, uniform convergence). Chapter 1 briefly recalls the measure and integration we need.

Contents

  1. The Big Picture: What Functional Analysis Does
  2. Background: Measure and Integration
  3. Lᵖ Spaces and Normed Linear Spaces
  4. Completeness and Separability
  5. Topological and Metric Spaces
  6. Linear Operators and Comparing Topologies
  7. Equicontinuity and the Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem
  8. The Baire Category Theorem and Its Applications
  9. Finite vs. Infinite Dimensions; the Open Mapping Theorem
  10. Dual Spaces and Weak Topologies
  11. The Hahn–Banach Theorem and Separation of Convex Sets
  12. Looking Back: the Main Thread

Notation

  • m is Lebesgue measure and m^* outer measure; "a.e." means almost everywhere.
  • Unless stated otherwise, function spaces live on [0,1]: L^p=L^p[0,1], and C[0,1] carries the max norm \|f\|=\max|f|.
  • B(x,r)=\{y:d(x,y)<r\} is an open ball; \bar A is the closure and \operatorname{Int}A the interior.
  • X^* is the (continuous) dual of a normed space X and X^\# its algebraic dual; L(X,Y) is the space of bounded linear operators X\to Y.
  • p,q are conjugate exponents when \frac1p+\frac1q=1.

0. The Big Picture: What Functional Analysis Does

0.1 In One Sentence

Functional analysis is "linear algebra in infinite dimensions, plus analysis". It studies vector spaces whose elements are functions, and the linear maps between such spaces.

Why study spaces of functions? Because many problems in analysis are, at heart, "find a point in a function space":

  • solving a differential equation u''=f: among all functions, find a u satisfying the equation;
  • variational problems (shortest paths, least energy): among a family of functions, find the one minimising some quantity;
  • Fourier analysis: writing a function as \sum c_ne^{inx} is choosing a set of "coordinate axes" in a function space;
  • probability and statistics: random variables are functions, expectations are integrals, and L^2 is the space of random variables with finite variance.

Once functions are "points", geometric language becomes available: distance, length, angle, projection, convergence.

0.2 Three Things We Take for Granted in Finite Dimensions

In \mathbb R^n three good properties are so natural that we rarely notice them:

  1. All norms are equivalent: however we measure "size", we get the same notion of convergence.
  2. Closed bounded sets are compact (Heine–Borel): every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence. Many existence proofs rely on exactly this — build a sequence of approximate solutions, then extract a convergent subsequence.
  3. Linear maps are automatically continuous: matrix multiplication cannot blow up small inputs uncontrollably.

0.3 In Infinite Dimensions, All Three Fail

Finite dimensions Infinite dimensions (e.g. function spaces) Where in these notes
All norms equivalent Different norms give genuinely different convergence (|\cdot|_1 small while |\cdot|_\infty large) Chapters 2, 5, 8
Closed bounded sets compact The closed unit ball is never compact Chapters 4, 8
Linear maps continuous Unbounded (discontinuous) linear maps exist Chapters 5, 7

0.4 How Functional Analysis Responds

The whole subject can be read as a systematic response to these three failures:

  • Completeness replaces "limits always exist". We work in complete spaces (Banach spaces), just as we use the reals instead of the rationals. Completeness, combined with the Baire category theorem, yields the fundamental theorems: the uniform boundedness principle, the open mapping theorem, and (without needing completeness) the Hahn–Banach theorem.
  • Recovering compactness in specific spaces. The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem says which subsets of C[0,1] are compact: besides being bounded, the functions must be "uniformly non-wiggly" (equicontinuous).
  • Recovering compactness by weakening the topology. The unit ball is not compact in the norm topology, but if we only ask that "every linear measurement converges" (the weak/weak-* topology), the unit ball becomes compact again (Alaoglu's theorem).
  • Studying only bounded linear operators. For linear maps, bounded ⟺ continuous, which lets analytic tools join forces with linear algebra.

1. Background: Measure and Integration

Why start here? We want function spaces to be complete — limits of Cauchy sequences should stay in the space. Riemann integration cannot deliver this: a sequence of continuous functions that is Cauchy for \int|f-g| may converge to something that is not Riemann integrable at all. Lebesgue integration is exactly what fills this hole, just as the reals fill in the rationals. The convergence theorems of this chapter answer a question that keeps coming back: when may we swap a limit and an integral?

1.1 σ-Algebras and Lebesgue Measure

A family \mathcal A\subseteq2^X is a σ-algebra if X,\varnothing\in\mathcal A and \mathcal A is closed under countable unions and complements (hence also countable intersections).

  • Borel σ-algebra: the smallest σ-algebra containing all open sets.
  • Lebesgue σ-algebra: all Lebesgue measurable sets.
  • Lebesgue measure is countably additive on pairwise disjoint measurable sets, and the measure of an interval is its length: m(I)=\ell(I)=b-a.

Outer measure is m^*(E)=\inf\{\sum_n\ell(I_n):\bigcup_nI_n\supseteq E\}. E is measurable (Carathéodory's condition) if and only if m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\cap E^c) for every set A.

1.2 Approximating Measurable Sets

Theorem: for E\subseteq\mathbb R the following are equivalent:

  1. E is measurable;
  2. for every \varepsilon>0 there is an open G\supseteq E with m^*(G\setminus E)<\varepsilon;
  3. there is a G_\delta set G'\supseteq E with m^*(G'\setminus E)=0;
  4. for every \varepsilon>0 there is a closed F\subseteq E with m^*(E\setminus F)<\varepsilon;
  5. there is an F_\sigma set F'\subseteq E with m^*(E\setminus F')=0.

Idea of (0)⇒(1): by definition of outer measure there are intervals \{I_n\} covering E with \sum\ell(I_n)<m^*(E)+\varepsilon; take G=\bigcup I_n (slightly enlarged to open intervals). This works when m(E)<\infty; in general, split E into countably many pieces of finite measure.

(1)⇒(2): take open G_k\supseteq E with m^*(G_k\setminus E)<1/k and G'=\bigcap_kG_k; then G' is G_\delta and m^*(G'\setminus E)=0. Hence E=G'\setminus(G'\setminus E): a measurable set differs from a Borel set by a null set.

1.3 Littlewood's Three Principles

  1. Every measurable set is nearly a finite union of intervals.
  2. Every measurable function is nearly continuous (Luzin's theorem): if f is measurable on E and finite a.e., then for every \varepsilon>0 there are a closed F\subseteq E with m(E\setminus F)<\varepsilon and a continuous g on E with g=f on F. If |f|\le M a.e., we may also take |g|\le M.
  3. Every convergent sequence of measurable functions is nearly uniformly convergent (Egorov's theorem): if m(E)<\infty and f_n\to f a.e., then for every \varepsilon>0 there is A\subseteq E with m(E\setminus A)<\varepsilon on which f_n\to f uniformly.

1.4 Convergence Theorems for Integrals

Assume m(E)<\infty (needed for (0) and (1)).

  1. Uniform convergence: f_n\to f uniformly implies \int f_n\to\int f.
  2. Bounded convergence theorem: |f_n|\le M and f_n\to f a.e. imply \int f_n\to\int f.
  3. Monotone convergence theorem (MCT): 0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots and f_n\to f a.e. imply \int f_n\to\int f.
  4. Dominated convergence theorem (DCT): |f_n|\le g with g integrable and f_n\to f a.e. imply \int f_n\to\int f.
  5. Generalised DCT: |f_n|\le g_n with g_n integrable, g_n\to g a.e., \int g_n\to\int g<\infty and f_n\to f a.e. imply \int f_n\to\int f.

Fatou's lemma: if f_n\ge0 and f_n\to f a.e., then \int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n.

Proof of the DCT: apply Fatou to the non-negative sequences g+f_n and g-f_n to get \int f\le\liminf\int f_n and \int f\ge\limsup\int f_n.

Two useful facts:

  • If f\ge0 and \int f=0, then f=0 a.e.
  • Absolute continuity of the integral: if f is integrable, then for every \varepsilon>0 there is \delta>0 with \int_A|f|<\varepsilon whenever m(A)<\delta.

2. Lᵖ Spaces and Normed Linear Spaces

Intuition. A norm is a ruler for the "size" of a function, and different p pay attention to different things: \|f\|_1 is the average height, \|f\|_2 the "energy", \|f\|_\infty the worst-case height. The larger p, the more spikes matter. On an interval of finite length, controlling a large-p norm automatically controls the smaller ones, so the spaces are nested. Another key point: once functions are vectors, "f is small" only makes sense once we say which ruler we use — irrelevant in finite dimensions, crucial here.

2.1 The Lᵖ Spaces

For 1\le p<\infty:

L^p[0,1]=\Big\{f\text{ measurable}:\int_0^1|f|^p<\infty\Big\},\qquad\|f\|_p=\Big(\int_0^1|f|^p\Big)^{1/p}.

For p=\infty: L^\infty=\{f:\exists M,\ m\{|f|>M\}=0\} (essentially bounded functions), with

\|f\|_\infty=\inf\{M:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}\quad(\text{essential supremum}).

Minkowski's inequality \|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p shows that L^p is closed under addition.

2.2 Linear Spaces and Norms

A linear space satisfies the usual axioms: a zero vector and additive inverses, commutative and associative addition, distributive scalar multiplication, and so on.

  • \{f\in C[0,1]:f(0)=0\} is a linear subspace of C[0,1]; \{f:f(0)=1\} is not (it does not contain 0).
  • Functions \{1,\dots,n\}\to\mathbb R correspond exactly to \mathbb R^n: a function can be viewed as an "infinite-dimensional vector".

A norm \|\cdot\|:X\to\mathbb R satisfies:

  1. \|x\|\ge0, with \|x\|=0\iff x=0;
  2. \|ax\|=|a|\,\|x\|;
  3. \|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|.

Examples: |x| on \mathbb R; \sqrt{x^2+y^2} or \max\{|x|,|y|\} on \mathbb R^2.

\|\cdot\|_p is only a seminorm: it satisfies 2 and 3, but \|f\|_p=0 only gives f=0 a.e. So the elements of L^p are really equivalence classes of functions that agree a.e., and on these \|\cdot\|_p is a norm. C[0,1] with the max norm can be viewed as a subspace of L^\infty: C[0,1]\subseteq L^\infty.

A handy identity: \|f^n\|_p=\|f\|_{np}^n.

2.3 Hölder's Inequality and Inclusions between Lᵖ Spaces

Hölder's inequality: for p,q\in[1,\infty] with \frac1p+\frac1q=1, f\in L^p and g\in L^q, we have fg\in L^1 and

\|fg\|_1=\int|fg|\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.

Generalisation: if \frac1p+\frac1q=\frac1r, then \|fg\|_r\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.

On [0,1], take g\equiv1 (\|g\|_q=1): for p>r, \|f\|_r\le\|f\|_p, so L^p\subset L^r:

L^1\supset L^2\supset L^3\supset\cdots\supset L^\infty\supset C[0,1].

Each later space is a linear subspace of the earlier ones. Note that (L^3,\|\cdot\|_2) is a normed subspace of L^2 (with the L^2 norm), but it is not complete (Section 3.3).

Finer inclusions (all strict):

  • L^\infty\subsetneq\bigcap_{1\le p<\infty}L^p (e.g. \ln x lies in every L^p but is unbounded);
  • L^q\subsetneq\bigcap_{1\le p<q}L^p and L^q\supsetneq\bigcup_{p>q}L^p.
  • If f\in L^\infty, then \|f\|_p\to\|f\|_\infty as p\to\infty; also \|f\|_p\to\|f\|_q as p\to q.
  • Being Cauchy in every L^p (p<\infty) does not imply being Cauchy in L^\infty.

The norms cannot be compared in reverse: take f=100\,\chi_{[0,1/100]} and g\equiv1. Then \|f\|_1=\|g\|_1=1, but \|f\|_2=10 while \|g\|_2=1. So no constant C gives \|h\|_2\le C\|h\|_1 for all h.

3. Completeness and Separability

Intuition. Completeness asks whether limits stay in the space: does a sequence of functions that get ever closer to each other converge to some function in the space? Only in complete spaces does the argument "build approximate solutions, then pass to the limit" stand up. Separability asks how big the space is: can countably many simple elements (e.g. broken lines with rational nodes) approximate every element? Separability means that, although infinite-dimensional, the space can still be handled "numerically". L^\infty is not separable: measured by the worst case, the space is too large to be described by a countable set.

3.1 Completeness

In a normed space, d(x,y)=\|x-y\| is a metric. A sequence \{x_n\} is Cauchy if for every \varepsilon>0 there is N with \|x_m-x_n\|<\varepsilon for m,n>N. A space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges. A complete normed linear space is a Banach space.

Two simple facts: ① convergent sequences are Cauchy; ② a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.

Theorem: L^\infty is complete.

Proof: let \{f_n\} be Cauchy, with \|f_m-f_n\|_\infty<\varepsilon for m,n>N, i.e. |f_m(x)-f_n(x)|<\varepsilon outside a null set A_{mn}. The union A=\bigcup_{m,n}A_{mn} is still null. Outside A, \{f_n(x)\} is a Cauchy sequence of reals, which converges to some f(x) by completeness of \mathbb R. Hence for a.e. x,

|f(x)-f_n(x)|=\lim_{m\to\infty}|f_m(x)-f_n(x)|\le\varepsilon\quad(n>N),

so \|f-f_n\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\to0. Also \|f\|_\infty\le\|f_n\|_\infty+\|f_n-f\|_\infty<\infty, so f\in L^\infty. \blacksquare

(L^p for 1\le p<\infty is complete as well — the Riesz–Fischer theorem.)

3.2 Completeness of Subspaces

Proposition: let X be a complete metric space and Y\subseteq X. Then Y is complete \iff Y is closed in X.

  • ⇒: if points of Y converge to x\in X, they form a Cauchy sequence, which converges in Y; limits are unique, so x\in Y and Y is closed. (This direction does not need X complete.)
  • ⇐: a Cauchy sequence in Y converges in X, and since Y is closed the limit lies in Y.

C[0,1] is complete: it is a closed subspace of L^\infty. If f_n\in C[0,1] and \|f_n-f\|_\infty\to0, then f_n\to f uniformly (after modifying f on a null set), and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (the \varepsilon/3 argument):

|f(y)-f(x)|\le|f(y)-f_m(y)|+|f_m(y)-f_m(x)|+|f_m(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.

3.3 Separability

A metric space X is separable if it has a countable dense subset A. The following are equivalent:

  1. \bar A=X;
  2. for every x and \varepsilon>0 there is y\in A with d(x,y)<\varepsilon;
  3. every non-empty open set meets A;
  4. for every x there are y_n\in A with y_n\to x.

Facts: L^p (1\le p<\infty) and C[0,1] are separable; L^\infty is not.

Proof that L^p is separable, in three steps.

① C[0,1] is separable. Let H be the set of broken lines that take rational values at the nodes k/n and are linear in between (union over all n); H is countable. Given f\in C[0,1]: f is uniformly continuous on the compact interval, so choose \delta with |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/4 when |x-y|<\delta, take 1/N<\delta, and pick g\in H with |g(k/N)-f(k/N)|<\varepsilon/4. On [k/N,(k+1)/N], g is linear, so its values lie between its endpoint values; hence |g(x)-f(k/N)|<3\varepsilon/4 and |g(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.

(A continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous: for each x choose \delta(x) with |f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/2 on B(x,\delta(x)); the balls B(x,\delta(x)/2) cover the compact set; take a finite subcover and \delta=\min_i\delta(x_i)/2.) Another countable dense set is the polynomials with rational coefficients (Weierstrass approximation theorem).

② C[0,1] is dense in (L^\infty,\|\cdot\|_p). Let h\in L^\infty with \|h\|_\infty=M. By Luzin's theorem there are a closed F with m([0,1]\setminus F)<\varepsilon and f\in C[0,1] with |f|\le M and f=h on F. Then

\|f-h\|_p^p=\int_{[0,1]\setminus F}|f-h|^p\le\varepsilon(2M)^p\to0.

③ L^\infty is dense in L^p. For l\in L^p take the truncations h_n=\max(-n,\min(l,n)). Then h_n\in L^\infty, h_n\to l a.e., and |h_n-l|^p\le|l|^p is integrable, so \|h_n-l\|_p\to0 by the DCT.

Together: H is dense in L^p, so L^p is separable. More generally, in the chain L^1\supset L^2\supset\cdots\supset L^\infty\supset C[0,1]\supset H, each later set is dense in the earlier ones under \|\cdot\|_p (p<\infty).

L^\infty is not separable: for \alpha\in[0,1] let f_\alpha=\chi_{[0,\alpha)}. Then \|f_\alpha-f_\beta\|_\infty=1 for \alpha\ne\beta. The balls B(f_\alpha,1/3) are pairwise disjoint and uncountably many, so no countable set can meet all of them.

A dense subspace that is not complete: L^3 is dense in (L^2,\|\cdot\|_2) and a proper subset. Take f\in L^2\setminus L^3 and f_n\in L^3 with f_n\to f in L^2; then \{f_n\} is Cauchy in (L^3,\|\cdot\|_2) but has no limit there. Also, if the whole space is separable, so is every subspace.

L^1\setminus L^2 is dense in L^1: take h\in L^1\setminus L^2; for f\in L^2, g_n=f+h/n\in L^1\setminus L^2 and g_n\to f in L^1; combine with the density of L^2 in L^1.

Convergence of series: if f_k\in L^\infty and \sum_k\|f_k\|_\infty<\infty, the partial sums satisfy \|S_m-S_n\|_p\le\sum_{k=n}^m\|f_k\|_p\le\sum_{k=n}^m\|f_k\|_\infty, so they are Cauchy in L^p, and by completeness \sum f_k\in L^p.

4. Topological and Metric Spaces

Intuition. A topology is the most general way to say "close": no distances, just a declaration of which sets count as open neighbourhoods. A metric is the special case with distances. The star of this chapter is compactness, the stand-in for "finite" in an infinite world: continuous functions attain their maxima on compact sets, sequences in compact sets have convergent subsequences, and many finite-dimensional arguments use nothing more. The chapter's key warning: in infinite dimensions, bounded no longer means "almost finite" — the unit ball can hold infinitely many points at mutual distance 1.

4.1 Topology

A topology on X is a family \mathcal T\subseteq2^X such that ① \varnothing,X\in\mathcal T; ② it is closed under arbitrary unions; ③ it is closed under finite intersections. (X,\mathcal T) is a topological space, members of \mathcal T are open sets, and an open set containing x_0 is an open neighbourhood of x_0. For any \mathcal C\subseteq2^X there is a smallest topology containing \mathcal C, the topology generated by \mathcal C.

  • U is open \iff each x\in U has an open neighbourhood V_x\subseteq U (so U=\bigcup V_x).
  • A is closed \iff A^c is open.
  • x_n\to x: for every open neighbourhood U of x there is N with x_n\in U for n>N.

Two extremes:

  • Trivial topology \{\varnothing,X\}: every sequence converges to every point.
  • Discrete topology 2^X: x_n\to x if and only if x_n is eventually equal to x.

Closure: \bar A=\{x:\text{every open neighbourhood of }x\text{ meets }A\}=\bigcap\{F\supseteq A:F\text{ closed}\}, the smallest closed set containing A; it contains all limits of sequences in A (in general topologies it can be larger; in metric spaces they agree). A is closed \iff A=\bar A. A is dense \iff \bar A=X \iff every non-empty open set meets A.

Continuous maps f:(X,\mathcal T_X)\to(Y,\mathcal T_Y): ① preimages of open sets are open \iff ② preimages of closed sets are closed \Rightarrow ③ x_n\to x\Rightarrow f(x_n)\to f(x). In general topological spaces ③ does not imply ① (in metric spaces they are equivalent).

Subspace topology: \mathcal T_Y=\{U\cap Y:U\in\mathcal T_X\}.

4.2 Compactness

  • Compact: every open cover has a finite subcover.
  • Sequentially compact: every sequence has a convergent subsequence.

Basic facts:

  1. A closed subset of a compact space is compact. (An open cover of A together with A^c covers X; take a finite subcover and drop A^c.)
  2. The continuous image of a compact set is compact; hence a continuous real function on a compact set attains its maximum and minimum.
  3. In metric spaces, compact \Rightarrow sequentially compact: if a sequence has no convergent subsequence, every point x has a ball B(x,\delta_x) containing only finitely many terms; these balls cover X, and a finite subcover contains only finitely many terms — contradiction.

4.3 Metric Spaces

A metric d:X\times X\to\mathbb R satisfies: ① d(x,y)\ge0 with equality iff x=y; ② symmetry; ③ the triangle inequality. The open balls B(x,\varepsilon) generate a topology \mathcal T_d; a topology \mathcal T is metrisable if \mathcal T=\mathcal T_d for some metric.

  • The trivial topology (on at least two points) is not metrisable; the discrete topology comes from the discrete metric d(x,y)=1\ (x\ne y).
  • On \mathbb R, 2|x-y|, \sqrt{|x-y|} and \frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|} are metrics; (x-y)^2 is not (no triangle inequality).

In a metric space: x_n\to x\iff d(x_n,x)\to0; \bar A=\{x:\exists x_n\in A,\ x_n\to x\}=\{x:\forall\varepsilon,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap A\ne\varnothing\}; the three forms of continuity (open preimages, sequences, \varepsilon-\delta) are equivalent.

Bounded vs. totally bounded: X is bounded if X\subseteq B(x,r); totally bounded if for every \varepsilon>0 finitely many \varepsilon-balls cover X. Totally bounded ⇒ bounded; in \mathbb R^n the two coincide.

Theorem: in a metric space the following are equivalent: ① compact; ② sequentially compact; ③ complete and totally bounded. If X is complete, then A\subseteq X is compact \iff sequentially compact \iff closed and totally bounded. In particular, in \mathbb R^n compact \iff closed and bounded (Heine–Borel).

Totally bounded ⇒ separable: for each n take a finite set A_n with \bigcup_{x\in A_n}B(x,1/n)\supseteq X; A=\bigcup_nA_n is countable and dense. Hence compact / sequentially compact ⇒ totally bounded ⇒ separable.

Bounded but not totally bounded:

  • The discrete metric on an infinite set: X\subseteq B(x,2) is bounded, but each B(x,1/2) contains a single point, so no finite family covers X.
  • The closed unit ball of L^\infty: the f_a=\chi_{[0,a]} are pairwise at distance 1.
  • The closed unit ball of C[0,1]: tent functions with disjoint supports are pairwise at distance 1.
  • The closed unit ball of L^p: similar square-wave functions are pairwise at a fixed positive distance.

So none of these closed unit balls is compact — a general phenomenon in infinite dimensions (Chapter 8).

Levels of continuity: Lipschitz (d_Y(f(x_1),f(x_2))\le Cd_X(x_1,x_2)) ⇒ uniformly continuous (\delta independent of the point) ⇒ continuous. A continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

4.4 Open and Closed Sets in Normed Spaces

In a normed space B(x,\varepsilon)=\{y:\|x-y\|<\varepsilon\} and x_n\to x\iff\|x_n-x\|\to0.

Example (in L^p, with E=[0,\frac12]):

  • A=\{f\in L^p:f\le1\text{ a.e. on }E\} is closed: an L^p-convergent sequence has an a.e. convergent subsequence.
  • \{f:f<1\text{ a.e. on }E\} is not open: f=0 belongs to it, g=\chi_{[0,\varepsilon)} does not, yet \|g-f\|_p=\varepsilon^{1/p} is arbitrarily small; it is not closed either: f_n=1-\frac1n\to1.

5. Linear Operators and Comparing Topologies

Intuition. Linearity brings rigidity: a linear map that is continuous at a single point is uniformly continuous everywhere, and all we need to check is whether it sends the unit ball off to infinity (boundedness). The second half of the chapter compares two notions of "close": a stronger topology has more open sets, makes convergence harder and compactness rarer. We will exploit this trade-off repeatedly — deliberately weakening the topology to gain compactness.

5.1 Topological Vector Spaces

A linear space X with a topology in which translation x\mapsto x+y and scaling x\mapsto ax are continuous is a topological vector space. Every norm topology is one.

A linear operator T:X\to Y satisfies T(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha T(x)+\beta T(y). When Y=\mathbb R it is a linear functional. A linear homeomorphism is an isomorphism; if moreover \|T(x)\|=\|x\|, it is an isometric isomorphism.

5.2 Bounded ⟺ Continuous

T is bounded if there is M with \|T(x)\|\le M\|x\| for all x.

Theorem: for a linear operator T the following are equivalent:

  1. T is continuous at some point x_0;
  2. T is uniformly continuous (in fact Lipschitz);
  3. T is bounded;
  4. there are M and a non-empty open set U with \|T(x)\|\le M for x\in U.

Proof:

  • ①⇒④: \|T(x)-T(x_0)\|\le\varepsilon for x\in B(x_0,\delta), so \|T(x)\|\le\|T(x_0)\|+\varepsilon.
  • ④⇒③: suppose \|T(x)\|\le M on B(x_0,\delta). For z\ne0, x_0+\frac\delta2\frac z{\|z\|}\in B(x_0,\delta), so
    \Big\|T\Big(\frac{\delta z}{2\|z\|}\Big)\Big\|\le\Big\|T\Big(x_0+\frac{\delta z}{2\|z\|}\Big)\Big\|+\|T(x_0)\|\le2M,
    i.e. \|T(z)\|\le\frac{4M}\delta\|z\|.
  • ③⇒②: \|T(x)-T(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|. ②⇒① is obvious. \blacksquare

Contrast: in general topological spaces there is only continuity; in metric spaces we distinguish continuity, uniform continuity and Lipschitz continuity; for linear operators all of these coincide.

5.3 Comparing Topologies

If \mathcal T_2\subseteq\mathcal T_1 are topologies on X, we say \mathcal T_1 is stronger (finer, more open sets), equivalently \mathrm{id}:(X,\mathcal T_1)\to(X,\mathcal T_2) is continuous. Then:

  • convergent in \mathcal T_1 ⇒ convergent in \mathcal T_2;
  • compact in \mathcal T_1 ⇒ compact in \mathcal T_2;
  • open (closed) in \mathcal T_2 ⇒ open (closed) in \mathcal T_1; \overline A^{\mathcal T_1}\subseteq\overline A^{\mathcal T_2};
  • dense in \mathcal T_1 ⇒ dense in \mathcal T_2; (X,\mathcal T_1) separable ⇒ (X,\mathcal T_2) separable;
  • f:(X,\mathcal T_2)\to Y continuous ⇒ f:(X,\mathcal T_1)\to Y continuous.

The strongest topology is the discrete one 2^X; the weakest is \{\varnothing,X\}.

Comparing metrics:

Relation Meaning
d_1 stronger than d_2 \mathrm{id}:(X,d_1)\to(X,d_2) continuous
d_1\sim d_2 equivalent \mathrm{id} a homeomorphism, \mathcal T_{d_1}=\mathcal T_{d_2}
uniformly stronger / equivalent \mathrm{id} (and its inverse) uniformly continuous
Lipschitz stronger d_2\le Cd_1 for some C
strongly equivalent c_1d_1\le d_2\le c_2d_1

Examples (on \mathbb R): d_1=|x-y| and d_2=\sqrt{|x-y|} are uniformly equivalent but not Lipschitz equivalent; d_4=\frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|} is uniformly equivalent to d_1 and Lipschitz weaker (d_4\le d_1); the discrete metric d_5 is stronger than d_1 and Lipschitz stronger than d_4 (d_4\le1=d_5); d_6=\frac{|x-y|}{2+|x-y|} is strongly equivalent to d_4.

Comparing norms: \|\cdot\| is stronger than \|\cdot\|' \iff \mathrm{id} is continuous \iff \|x\|'\le C\|x\| for some C; they are equivalent \iff \mathrm{id} is an isomorphism. For example, on L^2[0,1], \|f\|_1\le\|f\|_2, so \|\cdot\|_2 is stronger than \|\cdot\|_1: \{f\in L^2:\|f\|_1<1\} is open for \|\cdot\|_2, and convergence in \|\cdot\|_2 implies convergence in \|\cdot\|_1.

5.4 Equivalence of Norms in Finite Dimensions

Theorem: any two norms on \mathbb R^n are equivalent.

Proof: it suffices to compare an arbitrary norm \|\cdot\|' with \|x\|_\infty=\max|x_i|. Writing x=\sum x_ie_i,

\|x\|'\le\sum|x_i|\,\|e_i\|'\le\Big(\sum\|e_i\|'\Big)\|x\|_\infty,

so \mathrm{id}:(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\to(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|') is continuous, and therefore x\mapsto\|x\|' is continuous on (\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|_\infty). The unit sphere S=\{\|x\|_\infty=1\} is compact, so \|\cdot\|' attains a minimum m>0 on S (0\notin S); hence \|x\|'\ge m\|x\|_\infty. \blacksquare

6. Equicontinuity and the Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem

Intuition. Since the unit ball of C[0,1] is not compact, we ask: which sets of functions are compact? Look at a counterexample: the x^n are all bounded, yet they get steeper and steeper and finally "break" at x=1, with no uniformly convergent subsequence. The trouble is that their "wiggliness" is not controlled uniformly. Equicontinuity supplies exactly this: all functions share one modulus of continuity. The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem says bounded + equicontinuous + closed is precisely compact. It is the key tool for proving existence of solutions to differential equations (Peano's theorem): build approximate solutions, show they are equicontinuous, extract a uniformly convergent subsequence.

6.1 The Question

In \mathbb R^n, compact \iff closed and bounded. In C[0,1], closed bounded sets need not be compact (the closed unit ball is not). The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem answers: what extra condition characterises compact sets in C[0,1]? The answer is equicontinuity.

Let X be a compact metric space and C(X) the continuous real functions on X with \|f\|=\max|f|; (C(X),\|\cdot\|) is complete (uniform limits are continuous).

6.2 Equicontinuity

A family \mathcal F\subseteq C(X) is equicontinuous at x if for every \varepsilon>0 there is \delta>0 such that d(x,y)<\delta implies |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon for all f\in\mathcal F simultaneously (one \delta for all). If \delta is also independent of x, the family is uniformly equicontinuous. On a compact space, equicontinuous implies uniformly equicontinuous.

  • A finite family is always equicontinuous; a finite union of equicontinuous families is equicontinuous.
  • Sufficient condition: a family of C^1 functions on an open set U with |f'|\le M is equicontinuous (uniformly Lipschitz).

Examples:

Family Equicontinuous?
f_n=1/n, f_n=x/n (on \mathbb R) yes
f_n=x^n (on [0,1]) no (at x=1); yes at every point of [0,1)
f_n=nx no
f_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}x^n (on [0,1]) yes: for n>N, $
f_n=\frac1n\sin(n^3x) (on \mathbb R) yes: $

6.3 Equicontinuity and Uniform Convergence

  • If continuous f_n\to f uniformly, then \{f_n\} is equicontinuous (the \varepsilon/3 argument).
  • If f_n\to f pointwise and \{f_n\} is equicontinuous, then f is continuous: |f(x)-f(y)|=\lim|f_n(x)-f_n(y)|\le\varepsilon.

Proposition: if X is compact and the f_n are continuous, then f_n\to f uniformly \iff f_n\to f pointwise and \{f_n\} is equicontinuous.

Proof (⇐): for each x choose N_x with |f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/3 for n>N_x, and \delta_x with |f_n(x)-f_n(y)|<\varepsilon/3 (all n) and |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/3 on B(x,\delta_x). Then |f_n(y)-f(y)|<\varepsilon for y\in B(x,\delta_x) and n>N_x. By compactness take a finite subcover B(x_i,\delta_{x_i}) and N=\max N_{x_i}. \blacksquare

6.4 The Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem

Theorem (set form): A\subseteq C[0,1] (max norm) is compact \iff A is closed, bounded and equicontinuous.

Theorem (sequence form): let X be a compact metric space and \mathcal F a family of continuous functions on X that is equicontinuous and uniformly bounded (there is M with |f(x)|\le M for all x,f). Then every sequence in \mathcal F has a subsequence converging in C(X), i.e. uniformly.

Three kinds of "bounded":

  • Uniformly bounded: \exists M with |f(x)|\le M for all x,f.
  • Pointwise bounded: \forall x\ \exists M_x with |f(x)|\le M_x for all f (e.g. f_n=x/n on \mathbb R).
  • Each function bounded: \forall f\ \exists M_f (e.g. f_n\equiv n).

Proposition: if X is compact and \mathcal F is pointwise bounded and equicontinuous, then \mathcal F is uniformly bounded. (For each x choose \delta_x with |f(y)|\le M_x+\varepsilon on B(x,\delta_x) and take a finite subcover.)

Arzelà–Ascoli lemma: if X is a separable metric space and \{f_n\} is an equicontinuous, pointwise bounded sequence of continuous functions, then some subsequence converges pointwise to a continuous function f.

It combines two lemmas:

  • Lemma 1 (diagonal argument): if D is countable and \{f_n\} is pointwise bounded on D, some subsequence converges pointwise on D.
  • Lemma 2: if D is dense in X and \{f_n\} is equicontinuous and converges pointwise on D, then \{f_n\} converges pointwise on all of X, and the limit is continuous.

Proof of Lemma 1: write D=\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}. \{f_n(x_1)\} is bounded, so it has a convergent subsequence f_{1,k}; from it extract a subsequence f_{2,k} converging at x_2; and so on. The diagonal subsequence f_{k,k} is, from the j-th term on, a subsequence of row j, so it converges at every x_j.

Proof of Lemma 2: for y\in X choose \delta with |f_n(y)-f_n(x)|<\varepsilon/3 on B(y,\delta) (all n). Pick z\in D\cap B(y,\delta); \{f_n(z)\} converges, so |f_n(z)-f_m(z)|<\varepsilon/3 for m,n>N. Then

|f_n(y)-f_m(y)|\le|f_n(y)-f_n(z)|+|f_n(z)-f_m(z)|+|f_m(z)-f_m(y)|<\varepsilon,

so \{f_n(y)\} is Cauchy and converges to f(y); by equicontinuity, f is continuous. \blacksquare

Road map of the theorem: compact ⇒ totally bounded ⇒ separable; separable + equicontinuous + pointwise bounded ⇒ a pointwise convergent subsequence; compact + equicontinuous + pointwise convergent ⇒ uniformly convergent.

Set form, ⇐: A is bounded and equicontinuous, so every sequence in it has a uniformly convergent subsequence; the limit f lies in A since A is closed. So A is sequentially compact, hence compact.

Set form, ⇒ (compact ⇒ equicontinuous): suppose A is compact but not equicontinuous at x: there is \varepsilon such that for \delta=1/n there are f_n\in A and y_n\in B(x,1/n) with |f_n(x)-f_n(y_n)|\ge\varepsilon. By compactness a subsequence f_{n_k}\to f uniformly, with |f_{n_k}-f|<\varepsilon/3 for k>L. Then

\varepsilon\le|f_{n_k}(x)-f(x)|+|f(x)-f(y_{n_k})|+|f(y_{n_k})-f_{n_k}(y_{n_k})|,

so |f(x)-f(y_{n_k})|>\varepsilon/3. But y_{n_k}\to x and f is continuous — contradiction. \blacksquare

Examples: \{f\in C[0,1]:|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|,\ f(0)=0\} is compact (closed, |f|\le1, 1-Lipschitz hence equicontinuous); \{f\in C[0,1]:|f(x)|\le|x|\} is not equicontinuous, so not compact.

7. The Baire Category Theorem and Its Applications

Intuition. The Baire category theorem says a complete space cannot be a countable union of "thin" (nowhere dense) sets. It looks like a small topological fact but is really an "existence machine": to show that elements with some property exist (or even that "most" elements have it), show that the counterexamples form a countable union of thin sets. Its first big application is the uniform boundedness principle: for a family of bounded linear operators, pointwise boundedness automatically upgrades to uniform boundedness — completeness turns "fine at every point" into "fine overall".

7.1 Nowhere Dense Sets and Dense Gδ Sets

x is an interior point of A if there is an open U with x\in U\subseteq A. A is open \iff A=\operatorname{Int}A.

Nowhere dense: A is nowhere dense if one of the following equivalent conditions holds:

  1. (\bar A)^c is dense;
  2. \operatorname{Int}(\bar A)=\varnothing;
  3. no non-empty open set U satisfies U\subseteq\bar A (A is not dense in any open set).

Related facts:

  • \operatorname{Int}C=\varnothing\iff C^c is dense. Such a C is called hollow. Nowhere dense ⇒ hollow, but not conversely (\mathbb Q is hollow but not nowhere dense).
  • A nowhere dense ⇒ (\bar A)^c open dense ⇒ A^c dense (not necessarily open).
  • U open dense ⇒ U^c nowhere dense.

Examples: a point, a finite set, \mathbb Z and the Cantor set are nowhere dense. The Cantor set is compact, perfect (no isolated points: \overline{K\setminus\{x\}}=K for each x\in K) and totally disconnected (any two points can be separated by disjoint open sets U\ni x, V\ni y with U\cup V\supseteq K).

Dense G_\delta set: V=\bigcap_nU_n with each U_n open and dense. A set containing a dense G_\delta set is residual.

A dense G_\delta set can have measure zero: list the rationals as r_1,r_2,\dots and let E_k=\bigcup_nB(r_n,\varepsilon/2^{k+n}), an open dense set containing every rational, of measure \le\varepsilon/2^k; then E=\bigcap_kE_k is a dense G_\delta set of measure zero.

7.2 The Baire Category Theorem

Theorem: let X be a complete metric space.

  1. If A_1,A_2,\dots are nowhere dense, then \bigcup_nA_n has no interior points (in particular \ne X). Such a countable union is a set of first category (meagre). Note: the union itself need not be nowhere dense.
  2. Equivalently: if U_1,U_2,\dots are open and dense, then \bigcap_nU_n is dense (not necessarily open).

Corollaries: a countable intersection of dense G_\delta sets is a dense G_\delta set; a countable intersection of residual sets is residual (and non-empty). So a set and its complement cannot both be residual.

Examples:

  • \mathbb Q, \mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q and countable subsets of \mathbb R are hollow.
  • \mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q=\bigcap_{r\in\mathbb Q}(\mathbb R\setminus\{r\}) is a dense G_\delta set; more generally \mathbb R\setminus C is a dense G_\delta set for any countable C.
  • The rationals are a countable union of nowhere dense sets (points), but not a G_\delta set.

Application: there is no continuous f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R with f(\mathbb Q)\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q and f(\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q)\subseteq\mathbb Q.

Proof: if there were, then

\mathbb R=\mathbb Q\cup f^{-1}(\mathbb Q)=\bigcup_n\{r_n\}\cup\bigcup_nf^{-1}(\{r_n\}).

Singletons are nowhere dense; f^{-1}(\{r_n\}) is closed (f is continuous) and its complement contains \mathbb Q, hence is dense, so it is nowhere dense too. Thus \mathbb R is a countable union of nowhere dense sets and has no interior — contradiction. \blacksquare

Application: a Hamel basis of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is uncountable (Section 8.4).

7.3 The Uniform Boundedness Principle

Lemma: let X be a complete metric space and \mathcal F a pointwise bounded family of continuous real functions on X. Then there are an open set U and M>0 with |f(x)|\le M for all x\in U, f\in\mathcal F.

Proof: E_n=\{x:|f(x)|\le n,\ \forall f\in\mathcal F\}=\bigcap_{f}f^{-1}([-n,n]) is closed, and X=\bigcup_nE_n by pointwise boundedness. By Baire, some E_M is not nowhere dense; being closed, it contains an open set U. \blacksquare

Theorem (uniform boundedness principle / Banach–Steinhaus): let X be a Banach space, Y a normed space and \mathcal F a family of bounded linear operators X\to Y. If \mathcal F is pointwise bounded (for each x there is M_x with \|f(x)\|_Y\le M_x for all f\in\mathcal F), then there is M with

\|f(x)\|_Y\le M\|x\|_X\quad\forall x\in X,\ f\in\mathcal F,\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\|f\|\le M.

Proof: apply the lemma to the continuous real functions x\mapsto\|f(x)\|_Y: there are B(x_0,\delta) and M' with \|f(x)\|_Y\le M' there. For z\ne0, x_0+\frac\delta2\frac z{\|z\|}\in B(x_0,\delta), so

\Big\|f\Big(\frac{\delta z}{2\|z\|}\Big)\Big\|\le\Big\|f\Big(x_0+\frac{\delta z}{2\|z\|}\Big)\Big\|+\|f(x_0)\|\le2M',

i.e. \|f(z)\|\le\frac{4M'}\delta\|z\| for every f\in\mathcal F. \blacksquare

7.4 The Operator Norm and L(X, Y)

L(X,Y), the bounded linear operators X\to Y, is a linear space under (\alpha f)(x)=\alpha f(x) and (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x). The operator norm

\|f\|=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{\|f(x)\|_Y}{\|x\|_X}

satisfies the norm axioms (e.g. \|f+g\|\le\|f\|+\|g\|). \|f\|=M means ① \|f(x)\|\le M\|x\| for all x and ② M is the smallest such constant.

  • \mathcal F\subseteq L(X,Y) is bounded (\|f\|\le M) \iff \mathcal F is equicontinuous (\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|).
  • An unbounded linear functional: on C[0,1] with the L^1 norm, T(f)=\int_0^1\frac{f(x)}x\,dx (where defined) is unbounded.

Theorem: if Y is complete, then L(X,Y) is complete.

Proof: let \{f_n\} be Cauchy with \|f_m-f_n\|<\varepsilon for m,n>N. Then \|f_m(x)-f_n(x)\|\le\varepsilon\|x\|, so \{f_n(x)\} is Cauchy in Y and converges to f(x). f is linear (limits preserve linear operations). Moreover

\|f(x)-f_m(x)\|=\lim_n\|f_n(x)-f_m(x)\|\le\varepsilon\|x\|,

so \|f-f_m\|\le\varepsilon, f is bounded (\|f\|\le\|f-f_m\|+\|f_m\|), f\in L(X,Y) and f_m\to f. \blacksquare

In particular, X^*=L(X,\mathbb R) is always complete; it is called the dual space of X.

8. Finite vs. Infinite Dimensions; the Open Mapping Theorem

Intuition. The dividing line between finite and infinite dimensions comes down to one question: is the closed unit ball compact? Riesz's lemma explains the geometry: in infinite dimensions, however many directions you have already picked, there is always a new one "almost orthogonal" to all of them (at distance close to 1), so the unit ball holds infinitely many mutually distant points. The chapter's other protagonist is the open mapping theorem: between Banach spaces, a bounded linear bijection automatically has a bounded inverse. In other words, if the equation Tx=y always has a unique solution, the solution depends continuously on the data — stability comes for free.

8.1 Direct Sums and Complements

A+B=\{x+y:x\in A,y\in B\} and A+x is a translate. If A,B are linear subspaces with A\cap B=\{0\}, we write A+B=A\oplus B (direct sum). If A\oplus B=X, B is a complement of A; then every z\in X is uniquely z=x+y (if x_1+y_1=x_2+y_2, then x_1-x_2=y_2-y_1\in A\cap B=\{0\}).

Theorem: every linear subspace A\subseteq X has a complement B (possibly as small as \{0\}). Complements are not unique: X=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\oplus\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\oplus\operatorname{span}\{e_1+e_2\}. The dimension of a complement of Y is the codimension of Y.

8.2 Linear Independence and Hamel Bases

  • \operatorname{span}A is the set of all finite linear combinations of elements of A; it is a linear subspace.
  • The elements of A are linearly independent if any finite relation \sum a_ix_i=0 forces all a_i=0 (A need not be a subspace; for infinite sets only finite combinations count). Otherwise some x_k=-\frac1{a_k}\sum_{i\ne k}a_ix_i.
  • Hamel basis: every linear space X has a subset H with ① \operatorname{span}H=X and ② H linearly independent. Example: \{1,x,x^2,\dots\} is a Hamel basis of the polynomials P.

8.3 Characterising Finite Dimension

Theorem: for a normed linear space X the following are equivalent:

  1. X is finite-dimensional;
  2. a Hamel basis H is finite;
  3. X=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_n\} (\dim X=n when the e_i are independent);
  4. X is isomorphic to \mathbb R^n (whatever the norm);
  5. the closed unit ball is compact; 5′. every closed bounded set is compact;
  6. all norms are equivalent;
  7. all norms are complete.

Corollary: every finite-dimensional linear subspace is closed. Finite-dimensional spaces of the same dimension are isomorphic.

The isomorphism: x=\sum a_ie_i\mapsto(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb R^n; since all norms are equivalent (Section 5.4), (X,\|\cdot\|)\cong(\mathbb R^n,|\cdot|).

The negation of ⑥ (inequivalent norms in infinite dimensions): take countably many elements \{e_1,e_2,\dots\} of H, Y=\operatorname{span}\{e_n\} and X=Y\oplus Y'. For x=\sum a_ie_i+x' (only finitely many a_i\ne0) set

\|x\|'=\max\{|a_1|\|e_1\|,\ 2|a_2|\|e_2\|,\ \dots,\ n|a_n|\|e_n\|,\ \dots,\ \|x'\|\}.

Then \|e_n\|'=n\|e_n\|, so the two norms are not equivalent.

8.4 Riesz's Lemma: the Unit Ball Is Not Compact in Infinite Dimensions

Riesz's lemma: if Y\subsetneq X is a finite-dimensional (more generally, closed) proper subspace, then for every \varepsilon>0 there is x_0\in X\setminus Y with \|x_0\|=1 and \|x_0-y\|>1-\varepsilon for all y\in Y.

Proof: Y is closed; take x_1\in X\setminus Y (an open set), so there is \delta>0 with B(x_1,\delta)\subseteq X\setminus Y, hence m=\inf_{y\in Y}\|x_1-y\|\ge\delta>0. Since \frac m{1-\varepsilon}>m, there is y_0\in Y with \|x_1-y_0\|\le\frac m{1-\varepsilon}. Let x_0=\frac{x_1-y_0}{\|x_1-y_0\|}. For any y\in Y,

\|x_0-y\|=\frac{\big\|x_1-\big(y_0+y\|x_1-y_0\|\big)\big\|}{\|x_1-y_0\|}\ge\frac m{\|x_1-y_0\|}\ge1-\varepsilon.\qquad\blacksquare

Theorem (Riesz): if X is infinite-dimensional, the closed unit ball B is not totally bounded, hence not compact.

Proof: take x_1\in B and Y_1=\operatorname{span}\{x_1\}; by the lemma pick x_2\in B with \|x_2-x_1\|>1-\varepsilon; with Y_2=\operatorname{span}\{x_1,x_2\} pick x_3 at distance >1-\varepsilon from both; and so on. This gives an infinite sequence in B with pairwise distances >1-\varepsilon, so infinitely many balls of radius \frac{1-\varepsilon}3 are needed to cover it. \blacksquare

Hamel bases and completeness: a Hamel basis of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is uncountable.

Proof: suppose H=\{e_1,e_2,\dots\} is countable. For x=\sum_{i\le n}a_ie_i set f_m(x)=m\,a_m\|e_m\|. Each f_m is a bounded linear functional, and for fixed x, \{f_m(x)\}\subseteq\{a_1\|e_1\|,2a_2\|e_2\|,\dots,na_n\|e_n\|,0\} is bounded — pointwise boundedness. By the uniform boundedness principle there is M with |f_m(x)|\le M\|x\| for all m,x; but for m>M, f_m(e_m)=m\|e_m\|>M\|e_m\| — contradiction. \blacksquare (For instance, the space of polynomials is not complete under any norm.)

8.5 The Open Mapping Theorem

f:X\to Y is an open map if it sends open sets to open subsets of f(X).

Open mapping theorem: let X,Y be Banach spaces and T a bounded linear operator. Then T(X) is closed \iff T is an open map.

Corollaries:

  1. T:X\to Y bounded and onto (between Banach spaces) ⇒ T is open.
  2. T bounded and bijective ⇒ T^{-1} is bounded, i.e. T is an isomorphism (inverse mapping theorem). (When T^{-1} exists, T is open \iff T^{-1} is continuous.)
  3. Equivalence of complete norms: if (X,\|\cdot\|) and (X,\|\cdot\|') are both Banach and \|x\|\le C\|x\|', then there is C' with \|x\|'\le C'\|x\|. Proof: \mathrm{id}:(X,\|\cdot\|')\to(X,\|\cdot\|) is a bounded bijection, hence an isomorphism by corollary 2.

In other words: if one norm is strictly stronger than another, they cannot both be complete.

8.6 Kernels and Linear Functionals

For linear T:X\to Y, \ker T=\{x:T(x)=0\} is a subspace; when T is continuous, \ker T=T^{-1}(\{0\}) is closed.

For a linear functional T:X\to\mathbb R: if T\ne0, pick x_0 with T(x_0)\ne0; then

X=\ker T\oplus\operatorname{span}\{x_0\},\qquad x=\Big(x-\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}x_0\Big)+\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}x_0.

The first part lies in the kernel. Uniqueness: if x=x_1+a_1x_0=x_2+a_2x_0, applying T gives (a_2-a_1)T(x_0)=0. So the kernel of a nonzero linear functional is a subspace of codimension 1 (a hyperplane).

Theorem: for a linear functional f:X\to\mathbb R the following are equivalent: ① f is bounded; ② f is Lipschitz; ③ f is continuous at some point; ④ \ker f is closed. (For general linear operators, ④ does not imply the others.)

9. Dual Spaces and Weak Topologies

Intuition. Duality means "knowing an object through measurements": a vector x is described by the values f(x) of all linear measurements f\in X^*, just as a solid is described by its projections in all directions. The weak topology judges closeness through these measurements only: x_n converges weakly to x if and only if every measurement f(x_n) converges to f(x). The price is a weaker convergence (functions oscillating ever faster can converge weakly to 0); the reward is that compactness returns — Alaoglu's theorem says the unit ball of a dual space is weak-* compact. The variational argument "take a weak limit, then show it is the solution" rests on this.

9.1 Dual Spaces

  • X^\#: all linear functionals on X (the algebraic dual);
  • X^*: all bounded linear functionals on X (the dual space), with \|f\|=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{|f(x)|}{\|x\|}.

X is finite-dimensional \iff X^*=X^\#. X^*=L(X,\mathbb R) is always complete. We can keep going: X^{**}=(X^*)^*, X^{***}, …

Pairing: f(x)=\langle f,x\rangle is a bilinear map X^*\times X\to\mathbb R: f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y) and (\alpha f+\beta g)(x)=\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x).

Natural embedding J:X\to X^{**}, J(x)(f)=f(x).

  1. J(x) is bounded: |J(x)(f)|=|f(x)|\le\|f\|\,\|x\|, so J(x)\in X^{**} and \|J(x)\|\le\|x\|.
  2. In fact \|J(x)\|=\|x\|: by the Hahn–Banach theorem (Chapter 10) there is f\in X^* with \|f\|=1 and f(x)=\|x\|.

So J is an isometric embedding (isometry = norm-preserving isomorphism; isomorphism = linear + homeomorphism). A surjective isometry between metric spaces is a homeomorphism. Since X^{**} is complete, if X is not complete then neither is J(X).

Reflexive spaces: X is reflexive if J(X)=X^{**}. Reflexive spaces are complete.

9.2 The Dual of Lᵖ: the Riesz Representation Theorem

For g\in L^q (\frac1p+\frac1q=1), T_g(f)=\int fg is a linear functional on L^p. By Hölder, |T_g(f)|\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q, so T_g\in(L^p)^* with \|T_g\|\le\|g\|_q. Taking f_0=|g|^{q/p}\operatorname{sgn}(g) gives \frac{|T_g(f_0)|}{\|f_0\|_p}=\|g\|_q, hence \|T_g\|=\|g\|_q. So g\mapsto T_g is a linear isometric embedding L^q\to(L^p)^*.

Riesz representation theorem: for 1\le p<\infty and any T\in(L^p)^* there is a unique g\in L^q with T(f)=\int fg for all f\in L^p. That is, (L^p)^*\cong L^q.

  • The dual of L^1 is L^\infty; but the dual of L^\infty is not L^1 (Section 10.2).
  • L^p is reflexive for 1<p<\infty.
  • Finite dimensions: (\mathbb R^n)^*=\mathbb R^n, with f(x)=\sum a_ix_i.

9.3 Weak Topologies

Let \mathcal F be a family of real functions on X. The \mathcal F-weak topology \mathcal T_{\mathcal F} is the weakest topology making every f\in\mathcal F continuous; it is generated by \{f^{-1}(U):f\in\mathcal F,\ U\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ open}\}.

  • x_n\to x in \mathcal T_{\mathcal F} \iff f(x_n)\to f(x) for all f\in\mathcal F.
  • \mathcal F_1\supseteq\mathcal F_2\Rightarrow\mathcal T_{\mathcal F_1}\supseteq\mathcal T_{\mathcal F_2}.
  • \mathcal T_{\mathcal F}\subseteq\mathcal T \iff every f\in\mathcal F is continuous on (X,\mathcal T). In general the \mathcal F-weak topology and the original topology of X need not be comparable.

Examples: X=\mathbb R. With \mathcal F=\{\chi_{\mathbb Q}\}, \mathcal T_{\mathcal F}=\{\varnothing,\mathbb R,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\}; with \mathcal F=\{x\mapsto x\}, \mathcal T_{\mathcal F} is the usual topology.

Three weak topologies on a normed space:

Space Topology Generated by Convergence
X weak X^* x_n\rightharpoonup x\iff f(x_n)\to f(x),\ \forall f\in X^*
X^* weak X^{**} T(f_n)\to T(f),\ \forall T\in X^{**}
X^* weak-* J(X) f_n\overset{*}\rightharpoonup f\iff f_n(x)\to f(x),\ \forall x\in X

Weak- convergence is pointwise convergence.* Norm (strong) convergence ⇒ weak convergence ⇒ (on X^*) weak-* convergence. In finite dimensions the weak and norm topologies coincide. Accordingly we speak of weakly open, weakly closed, weakly compact sets.

Proposition: weakly convergent sequences are bounded.

Proof: x_n\rightharpoonup x means J(x_n)(f)\to J(x)(f) for all f\in X^*, so \{J(x_n)\} is pointwise bounded on X^*. Since X^* is complete, the uniform boundedness principle gives \|J(x_n)\|\le M, i.e. \|x_n\|\le M. \blacksquare

Weak convergence in L^p (1<p<\infty): f_n\rightharpoonup f \iff \int f_ng\to\int fg for all g\in L^q \iff ① \sup_n\|f_n\|_p<\infty and ② \int_Ef_n\to\int_Ef for every measurable E\subseteq[0,1]. (② is the case g=\chi_E; simple functions are dense in L^q, so ② plus boundedness suffices.)

Strong vs. weak convergence:

  • The square waves (Rademacher-type) r_n: \|r_n\|_p=1, no strong convergence, but r_n\rightharpoonup0.
  • f_n=2^n\chi_{(0,2^{-n})}\to0 a.e., but it does not converge weakly to 0 in L^p (1\le p\le\infty).

9.4 Helly's Theorem and Alaoglu's Theorem

Helly's theorem (the dual-space analogue of the Arzelà–Ascoli lemma): let X be a separable normed space and f_n\in X^* uniformly bounded (\|f_n\|\le M, equivalently |f_n(x)|\le M\|x\|). Then there are a subsequence f_{n_k} and f\in X^* with \|f\|\le M such that f_{n_k}(x)\to f(x) for all x\in X.

Proof sketch: \|f_n\|\le M ⇒ \{f_n\} is pointwise bounded and equicontinuous (|f_n(x)-f_n(y)|\le M\|x-y\|). By the Arzelà–Ascoli lemma (X separable) there is a pointwise convergent subsequence. The limit f is ① linear: f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\lim f_{n_k}(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y); ② bounded: |f(x)|=\lim|f_{n_k}(x)|\le M\|x\|, so \|f\|\le M. \blacksquare

Corollary: if X is separable, the closed balls \{f:\|f\|\le M\} of X^* are sequentially compact in the weak-* topology (not in the norm topology).

Facts:

  1. (For infinite-dimensional X) the weak-* topology on X^* is not metrisable;
  2. if X is separable, the weak-* topology restricted to B^*=\{f:\|f\|\le1\} is metrisable: \rho(f,g)=\sum_n2^{-n}|f(x_n)-g(x_n)| with \{x_n\} dense in the unit ball of X. Hence B^* weak-* sequentially compact ⇒ weak-* compact.

Alaoglu's theorem: for any normed space X, B^* is compact in the weak-* topology. (Compactness need not imply sequential compactness; for non-separable X, B^* may fail to be weak-* sequentially compact.)

Characterising reflexivity: for a Banach space X the following are equivalent: ① X is reflexive; ② the closed unit ball B is weakly compact; ③ B is weakly sequentially compact.

10. The Hahn–Banach Theorem and Separation of Convex Sets

Intuition. The duality theory of the previous chapter has a hidden risk: if X^* is too small (too few measurements), it cannot tell vectors apart and the weak topology is useless. The Hahn–Banach theorem removes the risk: a bounded linear functional on a subspace always extends to the whole space with the same norm, so there are "enough" measurements — any two points are separated by some functional. Its geometric form is even more vivid: a closed convex set and a point outside it can always be cut apart by a hyperplane. As a consequence, closed convex sets are also weakly closed, so taking weak limits inside convex sets is safe.

10.1 The Hahn–Banach Theorem

p:X\to\mathbb R is subadditive if p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y) and positively homogeneous if p(ax)=ap(x) for a>0.

Hahn–Banach theorem: let X be a linear space, Y\subseteq X a linear subspace, p non-negative, subadditive and positively homogeneous, and \varphi:Y\to\mathbb R a linear functional with \varphi(y)\le p(y) for all y\in Y. Then there is a linear functional f:X\to\mathbb R with

f(y)=\varphi(y)\ (y\in Y),\qquad f(x)\le p(x)\ (x\in X).

Proposition 1: if X is a normed space and x_0\in X, there is f\in X^* with \|f\|=1 and f(x_0)=\|x_0\|.

Proof: Y=\operatorname{span}\{x_0\}, \varphi(\lambda x_0)=\lambda\|x_0\|, p(x)=\|x\|. Then \varphi(\lambda x_0)=\lambda\|x_0\|\le|\lambda|\,\|x_0\|=p(\lambda x_0). Hahn–Banach gives an extension f with f(x)\le\|x\|, and -f(x)=f(-x)\le\|x\|, so |f(x)|\le\|x\| and \|f\|\le1; since f(x_0)=\|x_0\|, \|f\|=1. \blacksquare

Hence \|J(x_0)\|=\sup_{\|f\|\le1}|f(x_0)|=\|x_0\|, completing the proof in Section 9.1 that the natural embedding is isometric.

Proposition 2 (norm-preserving extension): if Y is a subspace of a normed space X and \varphi:Y\to\mathbb R is bounded with |\varphi(y)|\le M\|y\|, there is an extension f\in X^* with |f(x)|\le M\|x\|, so \|f\|=\|\varphi\|. Proof: take p(x)=M\|x\|.

10.2 Application: the Dual of L∞ Is Not L¹

Proposition: there is T\in(L^\infty)^* for which no g\in L^1 satisfies T(f)=\int fg for all f\in L^\infty.

Proof: on C[0,1]\subset L^\infty define S(f)=f(1). |S(f)|=|f(1)|\le\max|f|=\|f\| and S(1)=1, so \|S\|=1 and S\in(C[0,1])^*. By Proposition 2 there is T\in(L^\infty)^* extending S. If some g\in L^1 gave T(f)=\int fg, then for f_n=x^n,

1=f_n(1)=T(f_n)=\int_0^1x^ng(x)\,dx.

But |x^ng|\le|g| is integrable and x^ng\to0 a.e., so the right-hand side tends to 0 by the DCT — contradiction. \blacksquare

10.3 Convex Sets and Hyperplane Separation

K is convex if \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in K for x,y\in K and \lambda\in[0,1]. Intersections, sums K_1+K_2 and differences K_1-K_2 of convex sets are convex; unions generally are not.

Hyperplanes (affine subspaces of codimension 1): H is a hyperplane \iff there are a nonzero f\in X^\# and a\in\mathbb R with H=f^{-1}(a)=\{x:f(x)=a\}=x_0+\ker f (x_0\in f^{-1}(a)). A and B are separated by a hyperplane if some f satisfies \inf_{x\in A}f(x)\ge\sup_{y\in B}f(y) (strictly separated when the inequality is strict).

Hyperplane separation theorem: let X be a normed space, K a closed convex set and x_0\notin K. Then there is f\in X^* with

\inf_{x\in K}f(x)>f(x_0).

Corollary (Mazur): a convex set that is (strongly) closed is weakly closed.

Proof: for any x_0\notin A pick f\in X^* with a=\inf_{x\in A}f(x)>f(x_0). Then x_0\in f^{-1}((-\infty,a)), a weakly open set contained in A^c. So A^c is weakly open and A is weakly closed. \blacksquare

Summary: weakly closed ⇒ strongly closed (the weak topology is weaker); strongly closed + convex ⇒ weakly closed. In particular, closed linear subspaces are weakly closed.

11. Looking Back: the Main Thread

Back to the question of Chapter 0: how do we cope in infinite dimensions with the three things we took for granted in finite ones?

Counterexamples worth remembering — they mark the boundary of each theorem:

  • x^n on [0,1]: bounded but not equicontinuous, with no uniformly convergent subsequence.
  • \chi_{[0,\alpha]} (\alpha\in[0,1]): L^\infty is not separable and its unit ball is not totally bounded.
  • Tent functions, square waves: sequences in an infinite-dimensional unit ball that stay far apart.
  • Square waves r_n: weakly convergent to 0 but not strongly.
  • 2^n\chi_{(0,2^{-n})}: convergent almost everywhere but not weakly.
  • S(f)=f(1) extended to L^\infty: the dual of L^\infty is bigger than L^1.
